problem: VLN agents built for discrete nav-graph environments (R2R/RxR) cannot be transferred to continuous environments (R2R-CE/RxR-CE), because they depend on the connectivity graph for navigable directions and waypoints. Continuous agents that emit low-level actions (turn 15°, forward 0.25 m) trail same-architecture discrete agents by about 20% SR, and they cannot reuse discrete-VLN advances such as pre-trained VLN transformers.
motivation: Continuous navigation is closer to real robots, but low-level-action learning is implicit and expensive (episodes about 10x longer). A proof-of-concept study in Habitat shows that knowing navigable directions (view selection) is the main bottleneck. Moving a variable, structure-aware distance (waypoint teleportation) mainly adds efficiency. So supplying candidate waypoints at any position should recover most of the discrete-graph advantage.
key_idea: Train a panoramic RGB-D Transformer that predicts a local graph of accessible candidate waypoints at every step, using connectivity graphs re-fitted to Habitat-MP3D, so that unmodified discrete-VLN agents (CMA, Recurrent VLN-BERT) can navigate continuous environments by selecting a waypoint view that is then executed as low-level controls.
insight: Table 1 (GT graph in Habitat, val-unseen) shows the value lies in navigability rather than teleportation. Select-only (forward 0.25 m) reaches 37.72 SR, close to the full graph at 39.32. Teleport-only reaches 28.32 and pure low-level 27.29. Table 2 shows view selection helps at every fixed step length, but the best step length is scene-dependent, which motivates predicted waypoints. Table 4 shows that training on predicted waypoints matters, not only testing on them. CMA trained on the GT graph and tested with the predictor gets 29.92 SPL, while training with the predictor gives 33.90, matching the GT-graph agent (33.89). Waypoint augmentation lifts it further to 36.73, above navigating on the GT graph, by diversifying views and step lengths. Collisions drop from about 15% (fixed 1 m steps) to 7% with the predictor. The remaining failures come from missing waypoints at rare structures such as stairs.
method: Proof-of-concept analysis: isolates 'view selection' (choosing among navigable directions) from 'waypoint teleportation' (moving to a graph node) with an RCM/CMA agent in Habitat-MP3D, using panoramic input (12 views at 30°) in all settings.

Habitat-MP3D connectivity graphs: projects MP3D nav-graph nodes into Habitat and repairs invalid nodes and edges with heuristics. It samples 264 candidate positions within 0.35 m and scores them by obstacle clearance, number of added nodes and edge straightness. It adds detour nodes via shortest_path_follower, merges nodes closer than 0.5 m, and fits R2R-CE start/end points. Result: 13,358 nodes over 90 scenes, 3.31 edges/node on average, mean edge length 1.87 m, all in open space.

Candidate waypoint predictor: 12-view RGB and depth panorama encoded by frozen ResNet-50s (ImageNet RGB; DD-PPO PointNav depth) and merged per view. A 2-layer, 12-head Transformer attends only to the neighboring views. An MLP outputs a 120-angle (3°) × 12-distance (0.25–3 m) heatmap, trained with MSE against Gaussian-smoothed ground-truth heatmaps from the refined graphs (61 train scenes, 9,556 nodes). NMS keeps at most 5 waypoints.

High-level navigators in continuous space: the original CMA (GRU, trained from scratch) and Recurrent VLN-BERT (PREVALENT-initialized; state-refinement cross-modal matching removed) score the candidate-waypoint views. View features combine RGB, depth and cos/sin heading (replicated 32x). The selected waypoint is decomposed into low-level controls (turns in 3° increments, forward 0.25 m) executed in Habitat, with no teleportation.

Imitation learning: cross-entropy on the oracle waypoint and scheduled sampling that moves from teacher to student forcing every 5 epochs. On R2R-CE the oracle is the waypoint with the shortest geodesic distance to the goal. On RxR-CE it is the waypoint minimizing the geodesic distance agent→waypoint→sub-goal, where the sub-goal is the intersection of a 3 m ring with the GT path. Oracle stop fires within 1.5 m of the goal. Training runs on a single RTX 3090.

Waypoint augmentation: during agent training, a new waypoint is sampled from the heatmap patch of the selected view, so the agent sees diverse views, step lengths and obstacle interactions for the same instruction. It is disabled on RxR-CE, where no sliding is allowed; there a deadlock-escape heuristic is added.

setting.backbone: CMA (GRU seq2seq, trained from scratch) and Recurrent VLN-BERT (PREVALENT-initialized, fine-tuned). Frozen ResNet-50 RGB (ImageNet) and ResNet-50 depth (DD-PPO PointNav) encoders. Separate learned waypoint predictor (2-layer Transformer + MLP).
setting.training_data: Navigators: R2R-CE train (10,819 episodes) or RxR-CE train, one model per language on RxR-CE with multilingual BERT word embeddings. VLN-BERT is initialized from PREVALENT pre-training. Waypoint predictor: refined Habitat-MP3D connectivity graphs of the 61 R2R train scenes (9,556 nodes). No extra instruction augmentation data.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB-D (12 views at 30° separation, 224x224 RGB / 256x256 depth, HFOV 90)
setting.action_space: select one of ≤5 predicted candidate waypoints (120 headings × 12 distances, 0.25–3 m) or stop; the chosen waypoint is executed as low-level controls (turns in 3° increments, forward 0.25 m)
setting.privileged: none at test time for the main method (waypoints are predicted from RGB-D). GT-graph variants in the ablations use the ground-truth connectivity graph.

numbers_note: Several results are not transcribed above. (1) The proof-of-concept Tables 1–2 (RCM/CMA with GT connectivity graph, select/teleport and fixed-step variants on the filtered R2R-CE subset). (2) The waypoint-predictor metrics in Table 3 (MP3D val-unseen: |Δ| 1.40, %Open 79.86, d_C 1.07, d_H 2.00). (3) The GT-graph and frozen-predictor ablation rows of Table 4. (4) The appendix table comparing agents on MP3D vs Habitat-MP3D graphs. The RxR-CE val-unseen split is labelled only 'Unseen RxR' in the appendix and is assumed to be val-unseen. The intro claims '39% ... SPL on the benchmarking R2R-CE ... test sets', but Table 5 shows 36 SPL on R2R-CE Test-Unseen and 39 on Val-Unseen for VLN-BERT. R2R-CE numbers in Table 5 are rounded integers except TL/NE.
results: On standard R2R-CE, Ours (VLN-BERT) reaches 44 SR / 39 SPL on val-unseen and 42 SR / 36 SPL on test-unseen. The prior best, Waypoint Models, reaches 36/34 and 32/30, and CMA with predicted waypoints beats it on test by 6 SR / 3 SPL. This uses only imitation learning on 1 GPU for 3.5 days, versus DD-PPO on 64 GPUs for 5 days. On RxR-CE test, the agents reach 24.85 SR / 19.61 SPL / 37.30 nDTW (VLN-BERT), versus the VLN-CE baseline's 13.93 / 11.96 / 30.86. On the filtered R2R-CE set, predicted waypoints close the discrete-to-continuous gap: over low-level actions, SPL improves by 11.76 for CMA and 18.24 for VLN-BERT (val-unseen), and augmented CMA (36.73 SPL) exceeds CMA on the GT graph (33.89).
limitations: The predictor is fixed at ≤5 waypoints and a 2D planar graph. It misses waypoints at rare structures such as stairs, and the agent fully trusts the predictions, so missing or inaccessible waypoints cause failures and deadlocks (severe in no-sliding RxR-CE, where an ad-hoc escape heuristic is needed).
The predictor is trained only on graphs derived from MP3D annotations and is not language- or state-conditioned; transfer to out-of-domain scenes is untested.

RxR-CE runs change the official camera configuration (resolution/HFOV) and combine per-language models, and the R2R-CE gap analysis uses a filtered subset with re-derived shortest-path GT. Some numbers are therefore not strictly comparable to other work.
